Florence, early September. At the trattoria, over breakfast, Pietro, Graziella and Matei are reading the papers. They're all talking about the same thing.
Listen to this headline: "Farewell to the restorer who looked at paintings". It's Bellini!
Let me see. "Professor Bellini retires after forty years at the Uffizi."
Retirement… What an ugly word. It sounds like the headline of a funeral.
And here: "Handover in the Oltrarno: the workshop entrusted to two young restorers".
That's you! "Matei Popa and Giulia Esposito appointed to head the workshop."
"Young"… I'm thirty-five and I've got three grey hairs.
And look, there's a photo of Viola! "Workshop reopens: among the visitors, Italy's youngest restorer".
These journalists always exaggerate. Viola doesn't restore anything. At most, she looks.
Listen to this last one: "Florence. Farewell ceremony at the Uffizi, Friday at 6 pm. Mayor to attend. Free admission."
Because, for once, they're celebrating him and there's nothing he can do to stop it.
The language of the press, administration and science prefers nouns to verbs. Here's how the most common ones are formed:
English does the same: "to arrive → arrival", "to open → opening". But the suffixes differ, so learn the nouns together with the verbs.
Newspaper headlines cut everything that isn't necessary: articles, verbs, sometimes prepositions. The nouns remain:
Al via il restauro del Caravaggio.
È cominciato il restauro del Caravaggio.
Il professor Bellini va in pensione.
In Oltrarno il laboratorio passa a nuovi direttori.
"Al via" (from "dare il via" = to give the starting signal) is one of the most common formulas: "Al via i saldi", "Al via la stagione".
Very often the headline is a past participle placed first, without "è stato":
Hidden face discovered in the Caravaggio.
The participle agrees with the noun: "Scoperto un volto", "Scoperta una lettera", "Trovati i fondi", "Rinviate le lezioni".
Headlines use the present even for things that have already happened, to make them seem more vivid, and the future for plans:
The professor has left / leaves the Uffizi.
Il laboratorio aprirà anche la domenica.
The workshop will open on Sundays too.
In the body of the article, normal tenses return: passato prossimo, imperfetto, passive.
5. The passive and "si" in the news
Press articles use the passive and "si" a lot, to put the emphasis on the fact, not on who did it:
The appointment of the new directors has been announced.
According to reports, the ceremony will last an hour.

On Friday at a quarter to six, the corridor of the Uffizi was as crowded as on an August day. But this time there were no tourists. There were restorers from all over Italy, retired professors, students, journalists, the mayor with his tricolour sash, and a surprising number of people who had nothing to do with art: the baker from via Maggio, the pharmacist from Santa Croce, a taxi driver who said he had known the professor's father.

Bellini had arrived at half past five, perfectly on time, with the expression of a man being led to the scaffold. Matei and Giulia were waiting for him at the entrance, with Viola in their arms, wearing a little blue dress and a hair clip shaped like a paintbrush. "I asked you for one thing only," the professor grumbled. "No speeches, no flowers, no surprises." "No long speeches," Giulia corrected him. "We didn't promise anything about flowers or surprises."

The first surprise came at once. At the end of the corridor, by a window overlooking the Arno, were two figures Bellini recognised from afar: a small bald man in his black Sunday suit, and an elderly lady in a blue hat with a basket of lemons. Turi and Concetta had left Syracuse the day before, by train, "because lemons get spoiled on planes". Bellini stopped. For the first time since they had known him, he found nothing to say.

Then the others arrived. Doina and Ion, by train of course, with a jar of honey from Sibiu and a bottle that nobody needed to identify. Ilinca and Radu, on a belated honeymoon. Gennaro, who had promised not to bring fireworks and, for once, had kept his promise. And Dr Marini, from Rome, who shook Bellini's hand and said: "Professor, in 1995 you said no to us. Now I understand why."

In the second row, a little apart, were Chiara and Davide too. Chiara had started working at the workshop four days earlier, and in four days she had already learned three things: that Graziella's coffee is drunk at ten, not eleven; that Pietro is to be called "Doctor Guide"; and that Davide speaks only when he has something important to say. That evening Davide hadn't said a word. But under his arm he was holding a flat parcel, wrapped in newspaper.

The director of the Uffizi gave a short speech, as promised. Then the mayor gave a less short speech, as not promised. He talked about the 1966 flood, the Syracuse restoration, the open workshop, and announced Bellini's appointment as "honorary citizen of the Oltrarno", a title that until that day hadn't existed. Bellini listened to it all with his hands behind his back, staring at a spot on the ceiling.

Then it was Davide's turn. Nobody had asked him to speak, and he didn't speak. He went up to the professor with a parcel wrapped in newspaper, the page with the headline "Farewell to the restorer who looked at paintings". Inside was a pencil portrait: Bellini as a child, in his grandfather Ernesto's arms, in front of an enormous painting, copied from the old 1966 photograph. But Davide had added something. In one corner, very small, was another child, with a rucksack too big for him, watching the scene from a distance.

Bellini looked at it for a long time. Then he did something nobody had ever seen him do in public in forty years: he bent down and hugged someone. He hugged Davide, awkwardly, like a man who isn't quite sure where to put his arms. The newspaper photographer took a picture. The next day, on the front page, that photo would have a simple headline: "The handover".

While everyone was looking at the drawing, Viola climbed down from Giulia's arms and crossed the corridor on her own, toddling unsteadily across the shiny floor, between the guests' legs. She stopped in front of Bellini, looked up, pointed at the portrait and said, in her serious little voice: "Guadda!" The whole corridor burst out laughing. Bellini picked her up, something he had never done in front of anyone, and replied: "Yes, little one. I'm looking. I've learned."

At the end, when everyone was waiting for his speech, Bellini went up to the microphone and said only three sentences. "My grandfather taught me a rule: look, and don't touch anything. For forty years I have tried to teach it to others. Tonight I realised they have learned it better than I have." Then he turned to Matei and Giulia, took an old iron key out of his pocket and put it in their hands. "It's the key to the workshop. It was my grandfather's. Don't lose it."

The applause went on so long that the attendant had to remind everyone, timidly, that the museum closed at seven. Nobody listened. Ion opened his bottle in the corridor of the Uffizi, something probably forbidden by at least three laws, and poured everyone a finger of pălincă, the mayor included. "Noroc!" he said. And for the first time in the history of the gallery, two hundred people replied in Romanian.

Later, while the others were toasting, Bellini and Graziella found themselves alone at a window, watching the Arno flowing calmly under the Ponte Vecchio. "Sixty years ago, this water destroyed half the city," said Graziella. "And it brought a boy from Bologna together with an old restorer," Bellini replied. "Without that mud, I wouldn't be here. And neither would you." Graziella smiled. "Aldo would say the river knew what it was doing." They stood in silence, side by side, until the attendant switched off the lights.

That night, back home, Matei and Giulia hung the iron key on the shelf above the bed, next to Ernesto's small brush, Viola's new one, Ion's watch and the envelope with the two names. The shelf had been full for a long time, but they found a place for the key all the same.

The following Monday, Pietro took his class newsletter to school; he had become its editor. On the front page was an article he had written, with a photo of Bellini and Davide. He had chosen the headline after two days of thought, crossing out twelve others. It was short, as headlines should be. It said only: "A professor retires. A workshop doesn't."

Underneath, in small letters, Pietro had added a line his teacher had asked him to remove, because "a journalist mustn't put his own feelings into articles". Pietro hadn't removed it. It said: "P.S. Professor Bellini says that from now on he'll just be an old gentleman who looks at paintings. I don't think that's true. I think he'll go on watching all of us, and we'll pretend not to notice."
